summary.title: Einstein vs Maxwell: Is gravitation a curvature of space, a field in flat space, or both?
summary.field_subfield: Theoretical physics: gravitation, general relativity, relativistic theory of gravitation (RTG), cosmology
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical physics paper (analytical derivation and solution)
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a field-theoretic reformulation of general relativity (GTR) in which gravitation is treated as a field living in a fixed Minkowski background, and then extends it to the Relativistic Theory of Gravitation (RTG) of Logunov, which abandons general coordinate invariance through a bimetric coupling. The author, Theo M. Nieuwenhuizen of the Institute for Theoretical Physics at the University of Amsterdam, argues that the two seemingly opposed views of gravitation—Einstein's geometric curvature and Maxwell's field in flat space—are in fact equivalent, and that the field-theoretic approach is itself equivalent to a curved-space description, so both apply, describing the same physics from a different angle. The gravitational energy-momentum tensor is derived from the Einstein equations in a straightforward manner, allowing them to be presented as acceleration tensor = const. × total energy momentum tensor. For flat-space cosmology the gravitational energy is negative and cancels the material energy, so the total energy vanishes. The paper considers the case of a positive cosmological constant and solves a singularity-free version of the Schwarzschild black hole analytically. In the interior the components of the metric tensor quickly die out but do not change sign, leaving the role of time as usual. The ΛCDM model is covered for cosmology, while a form of inflation appears at early times. Here both the total energy and the zero point energy vanish. The paper traces the historical development from Einstein's step from flat space to curved space, through the quasi energy-momentum tensor problem, to the proper energy momentum tensor derived recently by Babak and Grishchuk, and to the bimetric theory of Nathan Rosen and the Logunov school. The author derives the acceleration tensor and the tensor τ µν in Minkowski space, which coincides with the Landau-Lifshitz quasi-tensor for Cartesian coordinates and with the Babak-Grishchuk tensor γtµν/g in general. The Einstein equations are written in the Newton shape acceleration = mass⁻¹ × force. The paper then applies the theory to cosmology, black holes, and the motion of test particles. For RTG with a negative cosmological constant it was claimed that an incoming spherical shell of matter is scattered off from a black hole; the author reconsiders this and shows that the present theory with a positive bimetric constant regularizes the interior of the Schwarzschild black hole, so escape is in principle possible and the theory allows a proper black hole. The modification of the Einstein equations involves the cosmological constant, so it is of Hubble size and immaterial for solar-system problems. In cosmology the theory directly leads to the ΛCDM model, while it could accommodate a positive curvature-like term. At short times there is a form of inflation. The gravitational energy exactly compensates the material energy, and the zero point energy vanishes, though the cosmological constant is finite and positive and is canceled by the bimetric terms. The paper concludes that curvature is a geometric description of the gravitational field in flat space, that clusters of galaxies do not move away from each other but the speed of light changes with cosmic time, and that the quantum version of RTG, if it exists, will involve quantization of fields but not of space. The paper notes that topics such as a realistic equation of state for black holes, classical tunneling of its radiation, regularization of other singularities, as well as aspects of the inflation and of inhomogeneous cosmology are under study. Executive Summary
This paper presents a field-theoretic reformulation of general relativity (GTR) in which gravitation is treated as a field living in a fixed Minkowski background, and then extends it to the Relativistic Theory of Gravitation (RTG) of Logunov, which abandons general coordinate invariance through a bimetric coupling. The author, Theo M. Nieuwenhuizen of the Institute for Theoretical Physics at the University of Amsterdam, argues that the two seemingly opposed views of gravitation—Einstein's geometric curvature and Maxwell's field in flat space—are in fact equivalent, and that the field-theoretic approach is itself equivalent to a curved-space description, so both apply, describing the same physics from a different angle. The gravitational energy-momentum tensor is derived from the Einstein equations in a straightforward manner, allowing them to be presented as acceleration tensor = const. × total energy momentum tensor. For flat-space cosmology the gravitational energy is negative and cancels the material energy, so the total energy vanishes. The paper considers the case of a positive cosmological constant and solves a singularity-free version of the Schwarzschild black hole analytically. In the interior the components of the metric tensor quickly die out but do not change sign, leaving the role of time as usual. The ΛCDM model is covered for cosmology, while a form of inflation appears at early times. Here both the total energy and the zero point energy vanish. The paper traces the historical development from Einstein's step from flat space to curved space, through the quasi energy-momentum tensor problem, to the proper energy momentum tensor derived recently by Babak and Grishchuk, and to the bimetric theory of Nathan Rosen and the Logunov school. The author derives the acceleration tensor and the tensor τ µν in Minkowski space, which coincides with the Landau-Lifshitz quasi-tensor for Cartesian coordinates and with the Babak-Grishchuk tensor γtµν/g in general. The Einstein equations are written in the Newton shape acceleration = mass⁻¹ × force. The paper then applies the theory to cosmology, black holes, and the motion of test particles. For RTG with a negative cosmological constant it was claimed that an incoming spherical shell of matter is scattered off from a black hole; the author reconsiders this and shows that the present theory with a positive bimetric constant regularizes the interior of the Schwarzschild black hole, so escape is in principle possible and the theory allows a proper black hole. The modification of the Einstein equations involves the cosmological constant, so it is of Hubble size and immaterial for solar-system problems. In cosmology the theory directly leads to the ΛCDM model, while it could accommodate a positive curvature-like term. At short times there is a form of inflation. The gravitational energy exactly compensates the material energy, and the zero point energy vanishes, though the cosmological constant is finite and positive and is canceled by the bimetric terms. The paper concludes that curvature is a geometric description of the gravitational field in flat space, that clusters of galaxies do not move away from each other but the speed of light changes with cosmic time, and that the quantum version of RTG, if it exists, will involve quantization of fields but not of space. The paper notes that topics such as a realistic equation of state for black holes, classical tunneling of its radiation, regularization of other singularities, as well as aspects of the inflation and of inhomogeneous cosmology are under study. Research Context
The general theory of relativity (GTR) was introduced by Einstein as a step from flat space to curved space. A fundamental difficulty is how to deal with the physics of gravitation itself, since there is only a quasi energy-momentum tensor. The proper energy momentum tensor of gravitation was derived only recently by Babak and Grishchuk. The Maxwell view that gravitation is a field in flat space was the starting point for Einstein and reappeared regularly. Changes of Einstein's GTR have mostly met deep troubles with one or another established property.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether gravitation is a curvature of space, a field in flat space, or both. The author hypothesizes that the field-theoretic approach to gravitation is by itself equivalent to a curved space description. The author predicts that when the theory is extended to RTG, the bimetrism forces to describe the Minkowski metric separately. The author predicts that a positive bimetric constant allows to regularize the interior of the Schwarzschild black hole. The author predicts that in cosmology the theory directly leads to the ΛCDM model. The author predicts that the gravitational energy exactly compensates the material energy.

Methodological Details
The study is a purely theoretical derivation performed by a single author at the University of Amsterdam. The approach starts with a field theoretic approach in Minkowski space. The Minkowski metric is denoted ηµν = diag(1, −1, −1, −1). The Riemann metric tensor is defined by rg γ gµν = γµν + hµν ≡kµν. The acceleration tensor is defined as Aµν = 1/2 DαDβ(kµνkαβ −kµαkνβ). The tensor τ µν is defined with the factor c4/(8πG). The Einstein equations are written in the Newton shape acceleration = mass⁻¹ × force. Cosmology is described by the Friedman-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric. The flat-space case is considered with k = 0 and U = 1, V (t) = a2(t). The relativistic theory of gravitation uses the Lagrangian LR = c4gµν/(16πG)(Gλ ·µνGσ ·λσ −Gλ ·µσGσ ·νλ). The extra gauge terms are Lg = LR −ρΛ + 1/2ρbiγµνgµν −ρ0√(γ/g). All second order derivatives drop out, leaving a bilinear form in first order covariant derivatives. Inserting the Einstein equations in the right hand side of (4) yields the Newton shape. The total energy momentum tensor is conserved, DνΘµν = 0, since Eq. (3) implies DνAµν = 0. The gravitational action is SR = ∫d³xdt√−g LR. The harmonic condition imposes u′ −v′ + 4w′ = r exp(v −2w). The geodesic equation is dvµ/ds + Γµ νρvνvρ = 0, with vµ = dxµ/ds. The differential proper time is dτ = √Udt and length dℓ= √V dr. The constant Ci is fixed at the initial position by Ci = √((1 −β²i)/Ui). The scale factor has an absolute meaning, and U = a6(t)/a⁴∗, V = a2(t). Going from cosmic time t to conformal time τ = ∫a³a⁻²∗dt yields the modified Friedman equation.

For flat space cosmology the total energy density is zero. The gravitational energy density is τ 00 = −3c⁴ ˙a²/(8πGa²), which is negative. The gravitational energy density cancels the material energy density T 00 = ρ. Such a universe contains no overall energy. The graviton has an imaginary mass and is a tachyon. The dimensionless small parameter is ¯λ = 2.38 × 10⁻²³ M/M⊙. The solution coincides with Schwarzschild's for ξ ≫1. Inside the horizon U and V decay very rapidly but remain positive. The brick wall width is ℓ∗/ℓP = 0.977 × 10⁻⁹/(1 + 0.019 log(M/M⊙)) M³/M³⊙. The approach makes sense only for M > 10³ M⊙. The time to see the shell hit the center is T = 2.74 × 10³² M/M⊙ yr. The minimal scale factor is zero, so a big bang can occur since ρbi > 0. The initial growth of the expansion is a = (a²∗cτ√(3Λbi/2))¹/³. The theory directly leads to the ΛCDM model. Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The field theoretic approach to gravitation is by itself equivalent to a curved space description. Both views apply, describing the same physics from a different angle. When the theory is extended to RTG, the bimetrism forces to describe the Minkowski metric separately. It is most natural to view gravitation as a field in flat space, which is Maxwell's view. Curvature is a geometric description of the gravitational field in flat space. Clusters of galaxies do not move away from each other, but the speed of light changes with cosmic time. The quantum version of RTG, if it exists, will involve quantization of fields but not of space. The separation of curved space into flat space and the gravitational field has implications for the quantum version.

Neither the Schwarzschild nor the Logunov black hole survives smearing of the central mass. The modification of the Einstein equations is of Hubble size and immaterial for solar problems.
